Surat Hud is Meccan, and it has one hundred and twenty-three verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book﴾: it is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate), or ﴿A Book﴾ is the khabar (predicate) of a deleted mubtada' (subject).

﴿Its verses have been made firm﴾ means they were arranged in a firm order, free from any defect in wording or meaning. Or they were protected from corruption and naskh (abrogation). What is meant is the verses of this surah, and there is no abrogated verse in it. Or they were made firm by proofs and evidences. Or they were made wise, a form taken from ḥukima (with a damma on the first letter) when something became wise, because it contains the foundations of wisdom, both theoretical and practical.

﴿Then they were detailed﴾ with benefits concerning beliefs, rulings, admonitions and reports. Or by being divided into sūrahs. Or by being sent down gradually, piece by piece. Or it explained in them and summarized what is needed. It was also read as ﴿thumma faṣṣalat﴾, meaning it distinguished between truth and falsehood and made its verses firm. The standard reading ﴿thumma fuṣṣilat﴾ has the verb built for the speaker. The particle ﴿thumma﴾ (then) indicates a difference in ruling or a lapse of time in the reports.

﴿From the presence of One who is All-Wise, All-Aware﴾ is another description of ﴿Book﴾, or a khabar after a khabar, or a ṣilah (complement) of ﴿made firm﴾ or ﴿detailed﴾. It affirms that its rulings and their detailing are arranged in the most complete manner fitting, with regard to what is manifest and what is hidden.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 11, verses 2–3:

﴿That you worship none but Allah.﴾ The *an* here is equivalent to *an lā* (so that you do not worship). It is said that *an* is *mufassirah* (explanatory, *an* serving to introduce an explanation), because the detailing of the verses carries the sense of speech. It may also be an independent statement, for exhortation to monotheism, or a command to disavow the worship of others, as if it were said: abandon the worship of other than Allah, meaning hold fast to this, or leave those things entirely. ﴿Indeed I am to you from Him﴾ from Allah. ﴿a warner and a bringer of good tidings﴾ of punishment for polytheism and of reward for monotheism.

﴿And that you seek forgiveness from your Lord﴾ is conjoined to *allā taʿbudū* (that you not worship). ﴿Then turn to Him in repentance﴾ then seek a means to your desired end through repentance, for the one who turns away from the path of truth must return. It is said: seek forgiveness for polytheism, then turn to Allah in obedience. It may also be that *thumma* (then) indicates the difference between the two matters. ﴿He will let you enjoy a good provision﴾ He will let you live in security and ease. ﴿until a specified term﴾ this is the end of your appointed lifespans, or He will not destroy you with the punishment of extermination. Provisions and terms are linked to lifespans, but they are specified in relation to each person, so they do not change. ﴿And He gives every doer of virtue his virtue﴾ He gives every person of virtue in his religion the recompense of his virtue in this world and the Hereafter, and this is a promise to the monotheist who repents of good in both abodes. ﴿But if they turn away﴾ and if you turn away (*tatawallaw*, with the second *ta* elided, as the original reading). ﴿then indeed I fear for you the punishment of a great Day﴾ the Day of Resurrection. It is said: the Day of hardships, when they were afflicted with famine until they ate carrion. It was also recited *wa-in tawallaw* from *waliya*.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 11, verses 4–5:

﴿To Allah is your return﴾: your return on that Day. It is *shādhdh* (anomalous) with respect to *qiyās* (analogical standard). ﴿And He is Powerful over all things﴾: so He is able to punish you with the most severe punishment. [p-128] It is as if this were a measure of the greatness of that Day.

﴿Unquestionably, they fold their breasts﴾: they fold them away from the truth and turn aside from it, or they incline them toward disbelief and enmity toward the Prophet ﷺ, or they turn their backs. It has been read as "yathnūnī" with the *yā'* and the *tā'*, from *ithnūnī*, which is a form of intensification (*mubālagha*). And "tathnūn," whose original form is "tathnūnan," from *al-thinn*, which is weak herbage. By this he means the weakness of their hearts, or the yielding of their breasts to folding. And "yathni'īn" from *ith na'anna*, like *ibyaḍḍa*, with a *hamza*, and "tathnawī."

﴿That they may hide [themselves] from Him﴾: from Allah, concerning their secret, so that He does not inform His Messenger and the believers of it. It was said that it was revealed concerning a group of polytheists who said: "When we lower our curtains, cover ourselves with our garments and fold our breasts over enmity toward Muhammad, how will He know?"

It was also said that it was revealed concerning the hypocrites, but this is open to question, since the verse is Meccan and hypocrisy emerged in Medina.

﴿Unquestionably, when they cover themselves with their garments﴾: unquestionably, when they retire to their beds and cover themselves with their clothing.

﴿He knows what they conceal﴾ in their hearts, ﴿and what they reveal﴾ with their mouths. His knowledge equally encompasses their secret and their open speech, so how could what they might manifest be hidden from Him?

﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾: of the secrets that are in the breasts, or of the hearts and their states.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 6:

﴿And there is no creature on the earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾. Its food and its sustenance, because He has undertaken it out of bounty and mercy. He used the wording of obligation ( wujub) to affirm that it will certainly reach it, and to urge reliance (tawakkul) upon Him in this. ﴿And He knows its place of settlement and its place of storage﴾: their places in life and in death, or in the loins (aslab) and the wombs (arham), or their dwellings on the earth when they come into existence in actuality, and their storage places from the materials and the seminal depositories when they were, previously, in potentiality. ﴿All﴾: each one of the creatures (dawabb) and its states. ﴿In a clear Book﴾: recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz). It seems that the verse intends to demonstrate that He is knowing of all that is known, and what follows demonstrates that He is capable of all possible things in their entirety, affirming monotheism (tawhid) and what preceded of promise and warning.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 7:**

﴿It is He who created the heavens and the earth in six days﴾: that is, He created them and what is in them, as its explanation has passed in "Al-A'raf" (the Heights, surah 7). Or it means what is in the two directions of up and down. He used the plural "heavens" but not "earth" because the heavenly bodies (al-'ulwiyyat) differ in origin and essence, unlike the earthly bodies (al-suflTyyat).

﴿His Throne was upon the water﴾ before their creation. Nothing stood between them. It does not mean that it was placed on the back of the water. From this verse it is inferred that a void (khala') is possible, and that water was the first thing created after the Throne among the bodies of this world. It has also been said that the water was upon the back of the wind, and God knows best. ﴿That He may test you as to which of you is best in deed﴾ is connected to ﴿created﴾. That is, He created that as the creation of one who creates, in order to deal with you as one who tests your conditions, how you act. The whole of that is causes and materials for your existence and your livelihood, and what your deeds require, and signs and indicators by which you reason and derive conclusions. The verb of testing (al-bala) may be linked to the word "which" because it contains the meaning of knowledge (al-'ilm), in that testing is a means to it, like looking and hearing. The superlative form and the word "test" are used to include all categories of the responsible (al-mukallafin) in terms of good and evil, to urge toward the finest of excellences, and to exhort constant advancement in the levels of knowledge and action. Here "action" means what includes the deeds of the heart and of the limbs. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Which of you has the best intellect, the most scrupulousness regarding the prohibitions of God, and the greatest haste in obedience to God?"

The meaning is: which of you is most complete in knowledge and action. ﴿And if you say, "You will indeed be resurrected after death," those who disbelieve will surely say, "This is nothing but clear magic."﴾ That is, the resurrection, or the saying of it, or the Qur'an which includes mention of it, is nothing but like magic in deception or falsehood. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "nothing but a clear magician" (sahir), so that the reference is to the speaker. It was also read "that you" (annakum) with a fatha, on the basis that "you said" (qulta) includes the meaning of "you mentioned." Or "that" (anna) may have the meaning of "upon" (ala), so that the sense is: "And if you say, 'Perhaps you will be resurrected,' meaning, expect your resurrection and do not decide by denying it, they would count it among what has no reality, as an exaggeration in denying it."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 8:

﴿And if We defer the punishment from them﴾ the promised punishment. ﴿until a counted community﴾ until a group of short periods of time. ﴿they will surely say﴾ mockingly. ﴿What holds it back?﴾ What prevents it from befalling. ﴿Surely, on the day it comes to them﴾ like the day of Badr. ﴿it will not be turned away from them﴾ the punishment will not be averted from them. The word "yawma" (day) is in the accusative, governed by the predicate of "laysa" (not), which is placed before it. This is evidence for the permissibility of placing the predicate of "laysa" before it. ﴿And there will surround them﴾ and it will encompass them. The past tense is used in place of the future to affirm the certainty of the event and for emphasis in the threat. ﴿what they used to mock﴾ that is, the punishment which they used to seek hastily. The verb ﴿yastahzi'un﴾ (mock) is used in place of "yasta'jilun" (seek hastily), because their hastening was a form of mockery.

﴿And if We let man taste mercy from Us﴾, and if We bestow upon him a blessing such that he finds its pleasure. ﴿Then We withdraw it from him﴾, then We strip him of that blessing. ﴿Indeed, he is despairing﴾, one who cuts off his hope in the bounty of God, the Exalted, due to the weakness of his patience and his lack of trust in Him. ﴿ungrateful﴾, one who is excessive in denying the blessing that had previously been bestowed upon him.

﴿And if We let him taste ease after hardship had touched him﴾, such as health after sickness, or wealth after poverty. There is a subtle point in the difference between the two verbs. ﴿He will surely say, "The evils have departed from me"﴾, that is, the calamities that troubled me. ﴿Indeed, he is exultant﴾, boastful over the blessings, deceived by them. ﴿and boastful﴾ toward people, preoccupied and distracted from gratitude and from fulfilling its due. The use of the words "letting taste" (adhaqa) and "touch" (massa) serves as an alert that what man experiences in this world of blessings and trials is like a model (unmudhaj) of what he will experience in the Hereafter, and that he falls into ingratitude and boastfulness at the slightest thing, because dhawq (tasting) is the perception of flavor, while massa (touching) is the beginning of contact.

﴿Except those who are patient﴾ in hardship, out of faith in God, the Exalted, and submission to His decree. ﴿and do righteous deeds﴾, in gratitude for His blessings, both past and future. ﴿Those will have forgiveness﴾ for their sins. ﴿and great reward﴾, the least of which is Paradise. The exception (istithna', "exception") here is from "man" (al-insan), since what is meant by it is the species; when it is marked with the definite article (al-), it conveys comprehensiveness (istighraq). Whoever takes it to refer to the disbelievers, because they were mentioned previously, makes the exception disjunctive (munqati', "disconnected").

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 12:

﴿Perhaps you would abandon some of what is revealed to you﴾ You would leave off conveying some of what is revealed to you, namely that which contradicts the opinion of the polytheists, out of fear of their rejection and mockery of it. But the expectation of a thing because of what calls for it does not necessarily entail its occurrence, since what turns one away from it, namely the infallibility of the prophets against betrayal in revelation and their trustworthiness in conveying it, may be present here. ﴿And your breast is constricted by it﴾ and there occurs to you at times a constriction of your breast, such that you would recite it to them out of fear, ﴿that they would say: "Why has not a treasure been sent down to him?"﴾ which he would spend in attracting followers, like kings do, ﴿or an angel has not come with him?"﴾ to confirm him. It has been said that the pronoun in ﴿by it﴾ is ambiguous and is explained by ﴿that they would say﴾. ﴿You are only a warner﴾ There is upon you only the warning with what has been revealed to you, and upon you is not [the obligation] that they reject it or propose [demands]; so why does your breast become constricted by it? ﴿And God is over all things a Guardian﴾ So rely upon Him, for He is Knowing of their condition and will requite them for their sayings and deeds.

(p-130) ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ *Am* here is *munqati'ah* (disjunctive, meaning "rather" or "or"), and the pronoun in *hu* refers to ﴿what is revealed﴾. ﴿Say: Then bring ten surahs like it﴾ in eloquence and excellence of composition. He first challenged them with ten surahs, then, when they were unable to do so, He made the matter easier for them and challenged them with a single surah. The singular *mithl* (like) is used in agreement with each individual surah. ﴿Forged﴾ means ﴿fabricated﴾ by yourselves. The sense is: if it is true that I fabricated it on my own, then you are Arabs, eloquent like me, and you are able to produce something like what I am able to produce. Indeed, you are more capable, since you have learned stories and poetry and are accustomed to verse and composition.

﴿And call upon whomever you can besides God﴾ for help in producing a counterpart. ﴿If you are truthful﴾ that it is invented. ﴿But if they do not respond to you﴾ by producing what you have called for. The pronoun is plural either to glorify the Messenger ﷺ, or because the believers were also challenging them. The Messenger's command also encompasses them, in that following him is obligatory for them in every matter, except what is specified by evidence. It also serves to alert them that the challenge is something that establishes the firmness of their faith and the strength of their certainty, so that they do not neglect it. For this reason He follows it with His words: ﴿Know that it was revealed with the knowledge of God﴾, accompanied by what none knows except God and none is able to do besides Him. ﴿And that there is no god but Him﴾; know that there is no god but God, because He is the Knower and the Capable of what no other knows and is able to do. This is also evident from the incapacity of their gods, and it is an explicit statement, whose truthfulness is established by its inimitability. It also contains a threat and a declaration of hopelessness that their gods could protect them from the punishment of God. ﴿Will you then be Muslims?﴾ That is, will you be steadfast in Islam, firm in it and sincere, once its inimitability is fully established for you? It is also possible that the whole address is directed to the polytheists, and that the pronoun in (*lam yastajibu*, "they do not respond") refers to *man istata'tum* ("whomever you can"). Thus the meaning is: if they do not respond to you by supporting you, because of their incapacity, and you have recognized in yourselves your inability to produce a counterpart, then know that it is a composition that none knows except God, that it is sent down from Him, and that what He has called you to, namely monotheism, is true. Will you then enter Islam after the decisive proof has been established? In such an interrogative form there is a powerful obligation, since it carries the sense of a demand and an alert that the reason has been established and the excuse removed.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 15–16:

﴿Whoever desires the life of this world and its adornment﴾ through his good deeds and his piety. ﴿We will pay them in full for their deeds therein﴾ We will deliver to them the reward of their deeds in this world, in the form of health, leadership, abundance of provision and a large number of children. It is also read as "yuwaffi" with the ya' (يُوَفِّ), meaning "Allah will pay them in full." It is read as "tuwaff" (تُوَفَّ) in the passive form, and as "nuwaff" (نُوَفِّ) with the lighter form and the raf' (nominative vowel), because the conditional verb is in the past tense, as in the line of poetry:

*"And if a generous man comes to him on a day of hunger... he says: 'My wealth has no absent part, and no forbidden portion.'"*

﴿And they therein will not be deprived﴾ they will not have any part of their rewards diminished. The verse was revealed concerning those who show off (ahl al-riya', people who perform deeds to be seen by others). It was also said that it concerns the hypocrites (al-munafiqun). It was also said that it concerns the disbelievers, their intentions and their piety.

﴿Those are the ones for whom in the Hereafter there is nothing but the Fire﴾ absolutely, in return for what they did, because they have received what their outwardly good deeds required, while the burdens of their evil intentions remain upon them. ﴿And what they did therein comes to nothing﴾ because nothing of reward remains for them in the Hereafter, or because there was never any reward, since they did not seek by it the face of Allah. The essential factor in earning its reward is sincerity (al-ikhlas). Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 17:

﴿Is he who has a clear proof from his Lord﴾ (burhan) from Allah, which guides him to the truth and rightness in what he takes and what he leaves. The hamza (interrogative particle) is for denying that one who has such a state should be equated with those who limit their aspirations and thoughts to this world, nor that they should be brought close to one another in rank. This is what dispensed with mentioning the predicate, and its estimated form is: "Is he who has a clear proof (bayyinah) like one who desires the life of this world?" This is a ruling that encompasses every sincere believer. It has also been said that what is meant is the Prophet ﷺ, and it has been said that it is the believers among the People of the Book.

﴿And a witness from Him recites it﴾: and that proof, which is the proof of reason, is followed by a witness from Allah who testifies to its soundness, and this is the Qur'an. ﴿And before it﴾: and before the Qur'an. ﴿was the Book of Moses﴾: meaning the Torah, for it too follows it in confirmation. Alternatively, the bayyinah is the Qur'an, and "yatluhu" is from recitation (tilawah), and the witness is Gabriel, or the tongue of the Messenger ﷺ, on the basis that the pronoun refers to him; or it is from "talw" (following), and the witness is an angel who guards it. The pronoun in "yatluhu" refers either to "man" or to "bayyinah" according to meaning. ﴿And before it the Book of Moses﴾ is a separate, independent clause. It is also read as "kitaba" in the accusative, in coordination with the pronoun in "yatluhu," meaning: a witness from among those who are upon a clear proof, indicating that it is true, reciting the Qur'an, like His saying: ﴿And a witness from among the Children of Israel testified﴾. It is also read "min qabli al-Qur'an" as "al-Tawrah" (the Torah).

﴿As a leader (imaman)﴾: a book followed in religion. ﴿And a mercy﴾ upon those to whom it was sent down, because it is the means of attaining success in the good of both abodes. ﴿Those﴾: a reference to those who were upon a clear proof. ﴿believe in it﴾: in the Qur'an. ﴿But whoever disbelieves in it among the factions﴾: from the people of Makkah and those who allied with them against the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. ﴿Then the Fire is his promised place﴾: he will enter it without doubt. ﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾: about the promise, or about the Qur'an; it is also read "muryah" with a damma, and both mean doubt. ﴿Indeed it is the truth from your Lord, but most people do not believe﴾: due to the shortness of their reflection and the corruption of their thinking.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 18–19:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who fabricates a lie against Allah?﴾ That is, he attributes to Him what He has not sent down, or denies of Him what He has sent down. ﴿They are the ones﴾, i.e., the liars. ﴿Who will be presented before their Lord﴾ on the Standing (al-mawqif, the Day of Reckoning), by being detained and having their deeds displayed. ﴿And the witnesses will say﴾ from among the angels and the prophets, or from their own limbs. "Witnesses" (ashhad) is the plural of shahid, like ashab (companions) is the plural of sahib, or it is the plural of shahid as in ashraf, the plural of sharif. ﴿These are the ones who lied against their Lord. Surely the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾: a great terror regarding what will befall them at that time because of their wronging themselves by lying against Allah.

﴿Those who bar from the way of Allah﴾, from His religion. ﴿And seek to make it crooked﴾: they describe it as deviating from truth and correctness, or they seek to make its people go crooked through apostasy. ﴿And they, of the Hereafter, they are disbelievers﴾: the meaning is that they are disbelievers in the Hereafter. Their repetition (of the pronoun "they") serves to emphasize their disbelief and its exclusivity to them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 20–22:

﴿Those are not ones who could escape (Allah) on earth.﴾ That is, they were not ones who could escape Allah in this world from His punishing them. ﴿And they had no protectors apart from Allah.﴾ Who could shield them from the punishment. But He delayed their punishment until this Day so that it would be more severe and more lasting.

(p-132) ﴿Their punishment will be doubled.﴾ This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf). Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read (yuda'af) with the doubling of the letter (ayn, i.e. yudda'af). ﴿They could not bear to hear﴾ because of their deafness to the truth and their hatred of it. ﴿Nor could they see﴾ because of their blindness to the signs of Allah. It seems that this is the cause of the doubling of the punishment.

It has also been said that this is an explanation of what was negated concerning the guardianship of the gods in His words: ﴿And they had no protectors apart from Allah.﴾ For that which neither hears nor sees is not fit for guardianship. And His words: ﴿Their punishment will be doubled﴾ are a parenthetical statement (i'tiradh).

﴿Those are the ones who have lost their own souls﴾ by exchanging the worship of Allah the Exalted for the worship of gods. ﴿And what they used to invent has forsaken them.﴾ That is, the gods and their intercession. Or: they lost through what they exchanged, and what they had gained was lost to them, so nothing remained with them except regret and remorse. Undoubtedly, in the Hereafter they are the greatest losers; there is no one more evident in loss and greater in it than them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 23–24:

﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds and humble themselves before their Lord﴾ (ikhbat, to submit humbly and be at peace with Him): they found tranquility in Him and submitted to Him, from al-khabt, which is the low, level land (al-ard al-mutma'innah). ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise; therein they will abide forever﴾: remaining eternally.

﴿The likeness of the two groups﴾: the disbeliever and the believer. ﴿Like the blind and the deaf, and the seeing and the hearing﴾: it is possible that what is meant is the comparison of the disbeliever to the blind, for his blindness to the signs of Allah, and to the deaf, for his deafness to hearing the words of Allah the Exalted and his refusal to ponder their meanings; and the comparison of the believer to the hearing and the seeing, because his situation is the opposite. Thus each of the two is likened to two things in terms of two attributes. Or the disbeliever is likened to one who combines blindness and deafness, and the believer to one who combines their opposites. The conjunction here serves to join attribute to attribute, as in the verse:

Al-sa'ih, fa-al-ghanim, fa-al-a'ib (the one who cries out, then the one who plunders, then the one who returns)

And this is of the type known as al-laff wa-al-tibaq (wrapping and antithesis).

﴿Are they equal?﴾: are the two groups equal? ﴿In likeness?﴾: that is, as an illustration, or as an attribute, or as a state. ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾: by drawing lessons from these examples and reflecting upon them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 27:

﴿So the eminent ones among his people who disbelieved said: "We see you only as a human being like ourselves."﴾ There is no superiority for you over us that would single you out for prophethood and make obedience to you obligatory. ﴿And we see none following you except the lowest of us﴾ (ajkhisa'una, "our base ones"), the plural of arhal (the lowest), for by common usage it has become like a proper noun, as in al-akbar (the greatest). Or arhal is the plural of radhl (base, despicable). ﴿Immature in judgment﴾ (badi al-ra'y), meaning apparent in judgment, without deep reflection, from al-badw (appearance), or first in judgment, from al-bad' (beginning). The yā' here is substituted for a hamzah because the letter before it is kasrah. Abu 'Amr read it with a hamzah, and it is in the accusative as an adverb of time, with the noun elided, i.e., "at the time of the emergence of the immature judgment," and the governing word is ﴿followed you﴾. They regarded them as base for this reason, or because of their poverty; for since they knew only the outward appearance of the worldly life (al-hayat al-dunya), the one who had the greater share of it was considered noble in their eyes, and the one deprived of it was considered base. ﴿And we see in you﴾, i.e., in you and in those who follow you, ﴿any superiority over us﴾ that would qualify you for prophethood and deserve to be followed. ﴿Rather, we think you are liars﴾: you in your claim to prophethood, and them in their claim to knowledge of your truthfulness. The addressee was thus given precedence over the absent party.

He said: "O my people, tell me: if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord," an argument bearing witness to the truth of my claim, "and He has given me mercy from Himself," by giving me the clear proof or prophethood, "but it has been made obscure to you," meaning it has been hidden from you, so it does not guide you. The pronoun is singular because the clear proof is itself the mercy, or because its being hidden entails the hiding of prophethood, or it is taken as referring to "it was made blind after the clear proof," with the reference omitted for brevity, or because the pronoun refers to each of the two separately. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read "fa-'ummiyat" (it was made obscure), meaning "it was concealed." It is also read "fa-'ammaha" (He made it obscure to you), with God as the subject. "Shall we compel you to accept it?" meaning, shall we force you to be guided by it, "while you dislike it?" meaning you do not choose it and you do not reflect upon it. Where two pronouns come together, neither of them being in the nominative case, and the more definite of them is placed first, the second may be either separated (al-fasl) or joined (al-wasl), as grammarians say.

"And O my people, I do not ask you for wealth in return for it," meaning in return for the delivery of the message. Although this is not mentioned, it is understood from what has been said. "My reward is only from God," for it is He from whom reward is hoped. "And I will not drive away those who have believed," this is an answer to them when they asked him to drive them away. "Indeed, they will meet their Lord," so they will dispute with their driver before Him, or, they will meet Him and triumph by being near Him, so how could I drive them away? "But I see you to be a people who are ignorant," of the meeting with your Lord, or of their worth, or in seeking to drive them away, or you are acting foolishly towards them by calling them "the lowly ones" (arādhil).

﴿He said, "Only Allah will bring it upon you, if He wills,"﴾ sooner or later. ﴿And you will not escape﴾ by averting the punishment or fleeing from it.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 11, verses 34–35:**

﴿And my counsel will not benefit you, if I wished to counsel you.﴾ It is a conditional clause (*shart*) whose response (*jawab*) is elided, and the clause itself serves as the indication of the response to His words: ﴿If Allah wills to lead you astray﴾. The sense of the speech is: "If Allah wills to lead you astray, then if I wish to counsel you, my counsel will not benefit you." That is why we say: if a man said to a woman, "You are divorced if you enter the house, if you speak to Zayd," and she entered, then spoke to him, she is not divorced. This is a reply to their implication that his disputation with them was speech without benefit. It also indicates that the will of Allah, exalted is He, may validly be connected to leading astray, and that the opposite of His will is impossible.

It has also been said that ﴿to lead you astray﴾ means to destroy you, from *ghawa al-fasil ghawan*, when the young camel overfills (with milk) and perishes.

﴿He is your Lord﴾: He is your Creator and the One who disposes of you according to His will. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾: so He will requite you for your deeds.

﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"? Say: If I have invented it, upon me is my crime﴾: its burden is on me. It has been read as *ajrami* in the plural (*ijrami* → *ajrami*, "my crimes"). ﴿And I am innocent of what you commit﴾: of your crime in attributing the fabrication to me.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 36–37:

﴿And it was revealed to Noah: "None of your people will believe except those who have already believed, so do not be distressed by what they have been doing."﴾ "Do not grieve and do not be sorrowful." ﴿by what they have been doing﴾ Allah Most High despaired him of their faith and forbade him to be grieved by what they had done of denial and harm.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 38–39:

﴿And he was making the ship⦆ — a narration of a past state. ﴿And whenever a group of the chiefs of his people passed by him, they mocked him.﴾ They ridiculed him for his building of the ship, for he was building it in a desert far from water, at the time of his might. They would laugh at him and say to him: "You have become a carpenter after you were a prophet." ﴿He said: If you mock us, then we mock you just as you mock⦈ — when the drowning overtakes you in this world and the burning in the Hereafter. It has also been said that the meaning of mockery here is ignorance-attribution (istijhal).

﴿So you will come to know who will receive a punishment that will disgrace him⦈ — by which he means them, and by the punishment he means the drowning. ﴿And there will descend upon him⦈ — and will alight upon him, or it will settle upon him like a debt from which there is no release. ﴿a lasting punishment⦈ — enduring, and this is the punishment of the Fire.

﴿Until, when Our command came﴾ is a limit (ghayah) for His saying ﴿and he was building the ark﴾, and what lies between them is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring back to the pronoun in it. Or ﴿until﴾ is the particle that introduces a new sentence after it. ﴿And the oven boiled over﴾: water gushed forth from it and rose up, like a cooking pot that boils over. The ﴿oven (tannur)﴾ is a bread oven, and the gushing began from it as a breach of the normal course of things. It was in Kufa, at the site of its mosque, or in India, or at the spring of Warda in the land of al-Jazira. It was also said that the tannur is the surface of the earth, or its most elevated place. ﴿We said: Load into it﴾, into the ship, ﴿from every﴾ kind of the animals that are useful, ﴿two of each pair﴾, a male and a female. This is according to the recitation (qira'ah) of Hafs, while the rest of the readers added, on the meaning of "load two," two from each category, a male and a female category. ﴿And your family﴾ is conjoined to "two of each pair" or to "two," and what is meant is his wife, his sons, and their wives.

﴿Except those against whom the word has already gone forth﴾, that they are among the drowned. This refers to his son Kan'an and his wife Wa'ila, for both of them were disbelievers. ﴿And those who believed﴾, and the believers from among others. ﴿Yet none believed with him except a few﴾. It was said that they were seventy-nine: his Muslim wife, his three sons Sam, Ham and Yafith, and their wives, and seventy-two men and women from among others.

It is narrated that he, peace be upon him, built the ship over two years from teak wood. Its length was three hundred cubits, its breadth fifty, and its height thirty. He made for it three decks: he loaded the beasts and the wild animals in its lowest part, the humans in its middle, and the birds in its uppermost part.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 41:

﴿And he said, "Embark therein"﴾ meaning: board it. He made this "riding" because it (the ship) on the water is like a mount on land. ﴿In the name of Allah shall be its course and its anchoring﴾ is connected with ﴿Embark﴾ and is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the waw (of the plural subject), meaning: embark therein, invoking the name of Allah, or saying "in the name of Allah" at the time of its sailing and its anchoring, or at its place of sailing and anchoring. The two words (majrā and mursā) are either a time, a place, or a verbal noun, with the modified noun (muḍāf) omitted, as in their saying: "I will come to you at the rising (khufūq) of the star." Their accusative case (naṣb) is by what we have supposed as a circumstantial clause. It is also permissible to make them nominative (raf') by ﴿In the name of Allah﴾, with the meaning of the two being a verbal noun, or a nominal sentence (jumlah) of subject and predicate, meaning: its sailing is "in the name of Allah," with "in the name of Allah" as the predicate or a complement, and the predicate omitted. It may be either an independent sentence unconnected to what precedes it, or a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) presumed from the waw or the pronoun (hā').

It is narrated that when he wanted it to sail, he would say, "In the name of Allah," and it sailed; and when he wanted it to anchor, he would say, "In the name of Allah," and it anchored.

It is also permissible that the word "name" (ism) is superfluous (muqḥam), as in his saying: "Then the name of peace be upon you both."

Ḥamzah, al-Kisā'ī and ʿĀṣim (in the transmission of Ḥafṣ) read ﴿majrāhā﴾ with a fatḥah, from "jarā" (to run). It was also read "mursāhā" from "rasā" (to anchor). Both readings admit of the three possibilities. And "mujrīhā wa-mursīhā" in the form of the active participle are two epithets of Allah. ﴿Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, meaning: were it not for His forgiveness of your lapses and His mercy upon you, He would not have saved you.

﴿And it ran with them﴾ is connected to an omitted element indicated by ﴿Embark﴾. So they embarked, saying the name of God, while it ran with them aboard it. ﴿Through waves like mountains﴾: through waves of the Flood, which is what rises from the water when it is agitated. Each wave in it was like a mountain in its piling up and its height. What is said, that the water covered everything between the heaven and the earth and that the ship was running within it, is not established. The well-known view is that it rose above the highest mountains by fifteen cubits. If that is authentic, then perhaps it was before the covering (taṭbīq, the enveloping of the earth by water).

﴿And Noah called out to his son﴾: Kan'an (Canaan). It was also read as "ابنها" (ibnahā) and "ابنهُ" (ibnahu) with the alif dropped, on the basis that the pronoun refers to his wife. He was her stepson (rabību). It was also said that he was born out of wedlock, on the basis of God's words: ﴿but they [both] betrayed them﴾. This is an error, since the prophets are protected from such things. The intended betrayal is betrayal in religion. It was also read as "ابناهُ" (ibnāhu) in the vocative of lamentation (nudba). Because it is a narration, the omission of the letter was permitted.

﴿He was in a place apart﴾: he had separated himself from his father or from his religion. Maʿzil is a noun of place (mafʿil) from ʿazala-hu ʿanhu, meaning to remove him far away.

﴿O my son, embark with us﴾: in the ship. Most readers pronounced the yā' with a kasra to indicate the omitted yā' of possession (yā' al-iḍāfa) throughout the Qur'an. Ibn Kathir is the exception: he paused on it in Luqman in the first instance by the agreement of the transmitters, and in the third instance according to the transmission of Qunbul and ʿĀṣim. Here he pronounced it with a fatḥa, limiting himself to the fatḥa of the alif that replaces the yā' of possession. The transmission from him differed in the other places. Abu ʿAmr, al-Kisa'i and Hafs assimilated the bā' into the mīm because they are close in articulation.

﴿And do not be with the disbelievers﴾: in religion and in separation.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 43–44:

﴿He said, "I will take refuge on a mountain that will protect me from the water."﴾ (i.e., from drowning me). ﴿He said, "There is no protector today from the command of Allah, except for the one on whom He has mercy."﴾ (i.e., except for the Merciful, who is Allah, the Exalted; or except in the place of those upon whom Allah has had mercy, who are the believers). By this he rejected that there would be today any refuge of a mountain or the like that protects one who seeks shelter in it, except the refuge of the believers, which is the ship. It was also said: "no protector" means "no one possessing protection," as in His saying: ﴿in a pleasing life﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:21]. It was also said that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "but whomever Allah has mercy upon, He will protect him."

﴿And the waves came between them﴾: between Noah and his son, or between his son and the mountain. ﴿So he became among the drowned﴾: so he became among those destroyed by the water.

﴿And it was said, "O earth, swallow your water, and O sky, withhold [your rain]."﴾ They were addressed with what those of understanding are addressed with, and commanded with what they are commanded with, as an illustration of the perfection of His power and their submission to what His creation wills in them, by a obeyed command that directs the one who submits to His ruling and hastens to comply with His order, out of awe of His greatness and fear of His painful punishment. Al-bal'(swallowing) is drying up, and al-iqla' (withholding) is restraining. ﴿And the water subsided﴾: it decreased. ﴿And the matter was decided﴾: and what had been promised of the destruction of the disbelievers and the deliverance of the believers was accomplished. ﴿And it came to rest﴾: and the ship settled ﴿on al-Judi﴾: a mountain in Mosul; it was also said in al-Sham; it was also said in Amol.

It is narrated that he boarded the ship on the tenth of Rajab and disembarked on the tenth of Muharram, so he fasted that day, and it became a sunnah.

﴿And it was said, "Away with the wrongdoing people!"﴾: destruction for them. It is said: "ba'uda ba'dan wa ba'adan," when he went far away, a distant going, such that his return is not hoped for. Then it was borrowed for destruction and specialized to curses of evil. The verse is at the peak of eloquence due to the grandeur of its wording, the excellence of its arrangement, and its indication of the reality of the situation along with conciseness free from defect. In reporting these events in the passive form there is an indication of the magnification of the Agent, and that He is definite in Himself and needs no mention, since the mind does not turn to anyone else, knowing that such acts are not within the power of anyone but the One, the Subduer.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 45–46:

﴿And Noah called out to his Lord﴾. He meant his calling out, as is shown by the conjunction of his words: ﴿He said: "My Lord, indeed my son is of my family"﴾, for that is the calling out. ﴿And indeed Your promise is the truth﴾: indeed every promise You make is true, admitting no failure, and You promised to save my family. So what is his state, or what is the matter with him that he was not saved? It is also possible that this calling out was before his drowning. ﴿And You are the most just of judges﴾: because You are the most knowing and the most just of them, or because You are more wise than the possessors of wisdom, given that the judge in terms of wisdom is like the armour-bearer in terms of armour.

﴿He said: "O Noah, indeed he is not of your family"﴾: this is to sever guardianship between the believer and the unbeliever. He alluded to this with His words: ﴿"Indeed he is one whose deeds are not righteous"﴾. For this is a justification for denying that he is of his family. Its origin is: "Indeed he is one of corrupt deed," and his very self was made the self of deed for emphasis, like the words of al-Khansa' describing a she-camel:

"She grazes as long as she grazes, until she becomes mindful, and then she is only advance and retreat."

Then he replaced "corrupt" with "not righteous," explicitly stating the contradiction between their two attributes and the absence of what would have made salvation obligatory for those of his family who were saved. Al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read ﴿"Indeed his deed is not righteous"﴾, meaning: he did a deed that was not righteous. ﴿So do not ask Me about that of which you have no knowledge﴾: about what you do not know, whether it is right or not. His calling out was named a question because it included mention of the promise of saving his family, a request for fulfilment regarding his son, or an inquiry into what prevented fulfilment concerning him. He called it ignorance and warned against it with His words: ﴿"I admonish you lest you be among the ignorant"﴾, because the exception of the one against whom the word had already gone forth from his family had already indicated the situation and made the question unnecessary; but love of the son occupied him from this, until the matter became confused for him. Ibn Kathir read with a fatha on the lam and a shaddah on the nun; likewise Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir, except that these two kasrah the nun, on the basis that the original is "tas'alanni," so the nun of protection (nun al-wiqaya) was deleted because of the gathering of nuns, and the shaddah was kasrah for the ya', then deleted, being satisfied with the kasrah. From Nafi', by the transmission of Ruways, it is also affirmed in connection.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 47–48:

﴿He said: "My Lord, I seek refuge in You from asking You about that of which I have no knowledge.﴾ In what is yet to come. ﴿And unless You forgive me and have mercy upon me, I will be among the losers.﴾ That is, if You do not forgive me for what has already passed from me in asking, and have mercy on me by granting repentance and bestowing favor upon me, ﴿I will be among the losers﴾ in deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 54–56:

﴿We say nothing except that some of our gods have struck you with evil.﴾ What we say is only our saying: "some of our gods have struck you" (i'tarak), meaning they have afflicted you, from 'arahu (to afflict) — ya'rūhu — when it afflicts him. ﴿With evil﴾ means with madness, because of your reviling them and your turning people away from them; and from that comes "tahdhi" (you rave) and "tatakallamu li-kharafat" (you speak nonsense). The clause is the object of the verb "say," and "illa" (except) is redundant (laghw), because the exception is "mufarragh" (an exception with no stated element before it).

﴿He said: Indeed, I call God to witness, and you bear witness that I am free from what you associate.﴾

﴿Besides Him, so scheme against me all together, then do not give me respite.﴾ He answered their foolish claim by calling God Most High to witness to his freedom from their gods and to his being free of any harm from them, as an emphasis and confirmation of that. He ordered them to bear witness against him, showing contempt for them, and to unite in plotting his destruction without delay, so that when they exerted themselves in it and saw that they were all unable, and they are the strongest and most powerful, to harm him, there would remain for them no doubt that their gods, which are inanimate objects that neither harm nor benefit, cannot harm him by way of retribution. This is among his miracles, for confronting a single man, by himself, the multitude of ferocious tyrants thirsting to shed his blood with this statement is nothing but due to his trust in God, and restraining them from harming him is nothing but by His protection of him. For this reason he followed it with his saying:

﴿Indeed, I have put my trust in God, my Lord and your Lord. There is no creature but that He holds its forelock.﴾ This is an affirmation of it, and the meaning is that even if you exert the utmost of your power, you will never harm me, for I rely upon God and am confident in His protection; He is my Lord and your Lord, and nothing befalls me except what He wills, and you cannot bring about what He has not decreed. Then he proved it by his saying: ﴿There is no creature but that He holds its forelock﴾, meaning that He possesses it and has power over it, directing it as He wills, and "seizing by the forelocks" is a figure of speech for this.

﴿Indeed, my Lord is on a straight path﴾, meaning that He is upon truth and justice; no one who seeks refuge in Him is lost before Him, and no wrongdoer escapes Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 11, verses 59–60:

﴿And those were ʿĀd﴾ The demonstrative noun (*ism al-ishara*, "that") is feminine (*unnitha*) in consideration of the tribe (*qabila*), or because the reference is to their graves and their traces.

﴿They denied the signs of their Lord﴾: they disbelieved in them.

﴿And disobeyed His messengers﴾: because they disobeyed their messenger, and whoever disobeys a messenger, it is as if he has disobeyed all of them, since they were commanded to obey every messenger.

﴿And followed the command of every obstinate tyrant﴾: meaning their great ones who transgressed. *ʿAnid* is from *ʿanada*, *ʿanadan*, *ʿindan*, *ʿunudan*, when he transgressed. The meaning is: they disobeyed the one who called them to faith and to what would save them, and obeyed the one who called them to disbelief and to what would destroy them.

﴿And they were made to follow up with a curse in this world and on the Day of Resurrection﴾: that is, the curse was made to follow them in both abodes, overturning them into punishment.

﴿Indeed, ʿĀd disbelieved in their Lord﴾: they denied Him, or they disbelieved His blessings, or they disbelieved in Him, and the preposition was elided (*hudhifa al-jarr*).

﴿Away with ʿĀd!﴾: a supplication against them for destruction. The purpose is to show that they deserved what descended upon them because of what has been related of them. He repeated *alā* (*ألا*, "indeed/away") and restated their name to magnify their affair and to urge reflection on their condition.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 64–65:

﴿And O my people, this is the she-camel of Allah, a sign for you﴾. *Ayatan* is in the accusative as a *hal* (circumstantial qualifier, indicating the state of the subject at the time of the action), and its governing element is the sense of pointing (*ma'na al-isharah*) contained in the demonstrative. *Lakum* is a *hal* of it (*minha*), placed before it because the noun it modifies is indefinite (*li-tankiriha*).

﴿So leave her to eat on the land of Allah﴾: she grazes its vegetation and drinks its water. ﴿And do not touch her with harm, lest a punishment seize you﴾ that is imminent, which will not be delayed after your touching her with harm except for a short time, namely three days.

﴿But they hamstrung her, so he said: Enjoy yourselves in your homes﴾: live in your dwellings, or in your worldly abode. ﴿For three days﴾: Wednesday, Thursday and Friday, after which you will perish. ﴿That is a promise not to be denied﴾: that is, a promise not to be lied about. The phrase has been extended by treating it as if it were the direct object (*maf'ul bihi*), as in the verse of poetry:

*And the day we witnessed him, Sulaym and ʿĀmir*

Or it means "not to be denied" in a figurative sense (*majaz*): it is as if the one making the promise said to him, "Will you fulfil it?"; if he fulfils it, the promise is confirmed, and if not, it is denied. Or it means "a promise that is not a lie," with *wa'd* taken as a verbal noun (*masdar*), like *al-majlud* and *al-ma'qul*.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 66–68:

﴿So when Our command came, We saved Salih and those who believed with him by mercy from Us, and from the disgrace of that Day.﴾ That is: and We saved them from the disgrace of that Day, which is their destruction by the Blast (al-sayha), or their humiliation and exposure on the Day of Resurrection. ﴿And those who did wrong were seized by the Blast, and they became prostrate in their homes﴾. The interpretation of this has already preceded in surah al-A'raf.

Yet, away with Thamud!﴾ Abu Bakr read it with tanwin here and in al-Najm, and al-Kisa'i in all of the Qur'an, and Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr in His saying: ﴿Away with Thamud!﴾, [treating Thamud as] referring to the tribe or to the great ancestor (al-ab al-akbar).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 69:

(p-141)﴿And indeed Our messengers came to Abraham with the good tidings﴾. He means the angels. It is said they were nine; and it is said three: Jibril (Gabriel), Mika'il (Michael) and Israfil (Raphael).

﴿with the good tidings﴾: with the good news of a son. It is also said: with the news of the destruction of the people of Lot. ﴿They said, "Peace"﴾: "We greet you with peace." It is permissible for it to be in the accusative (naṣb) governed by ﴿they said﴾, in the sense of "they mentioned peace." ﴿He said, "Peace"﴾: that is, your affair is peace, or my reply is peace, or "and upon you be peace," and he put it in the nominative (raf') as a response, with a better greeting than theirs. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sallama" (salama), and likewise in al-Dhariyat; both are dialects, like ḥarrama and ḥarām. It is also said that what is meant by it is reconciliation (ṣulḥ).

﴿So he did not delay in bringing a roasted calf﴾: that is, his bringing it was not slow, or he was not slow in bringing it, or he did not delay in regard to it. The preposition in ﴿an﴾ is either implied or elided. Ḥanīdh means roasted over hot stones (raḍf). It is also said: one whose fat drips, from ḥanaztu al-faras (I made the horse sweat), when I cover it with a blanket (jalāl), based on His saying: ﴿with a fat calf﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 70–71:

﴿When he saw their hands not reaching toward it﴾: they were not extending their hands toward it. ﴿He perceived them as strangers and felt fear of them﴾: he disapproved of that from them and feared that they intended him some harm. Nakira (perceived as strange), ankara (disapproved) and istankara (found strange) carry the same meaning. Al-iijas (perception) is the sensing, and it was said that it means concealing (the fear). ﴿They said﴾ to him, when they perceived from him the trace of fear: ﴿Fear not. Indeed we have been sent to the people of Lut﴾: we are angels sent to them with punishment. And the reason we did not extend our hands to him is that we do not eat.

﴿And his wife was standing﴾: behind the screen, listening to their conversation, or standing over them to serve. ﴿So she laughed﴾: out of joy at the removal of the fear, or at the destruction of the people of corruption, or at the correctness of her opinion, for she used to say to Ibrahim: "Take Lut to yourself, for I know that the punishment will descend upon these people." It was also said that "she laughed" means "she menstruated." The poet said:

"And my covenant with Salma was that she laughed in Lubaba... and her breast had not yet grown beyond what it had become firm."

From this comes the expression "the acacia laughed" when its gum flows. It is also read with a fatha on the ha' (faḥḥat, i.e., she menstruated). ﴿So We gave her good news of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾: Ibn 'Amir, Hamza and Hafs read it in the accusative, governed by a verb implied by the context, the estimated meaning being: "And We bestowed upon her, after Ishaq, Ya'qub." It was said that it is in apposition to the place of "bi-Ishaq" or to the wording of "Ishaq," and its fatha is for the genitive, since it is not declinable; it was admitted because of the separation between it and what it is conjoined to by the adverbial phrase. The rest read it in the nominative, as a subject (mubtada').

Its predicate is the adverbial phrase, i.e., "and Ya'qub is born after him." It was said that al-wara' means a grandson, and perhaps it was so named because he comes after the son; on this view, its attribution to Ishaq is not because Ya'qub is behind him, but because he is behind Ibrahim on his side. This requires consideration. The two names may occur in the good news, as with Yahya, and they may occur in the narration after both were born and were named accordingly. The directing of the good news to her is to indicate that the child promised would be from her and not from Hajar, and because she was barren and eager for a child.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 72–73:

﴿She said, "Woe to me!"﴾ That is, "O wonder!" Its origin is in evil, and then it was applied to every dreadful matter. It was also read as "Yā-ʾ" (ﻳَﺎ) in accordance with the original form.

﴿"Shall I give birth while I am an old woman,"﴾ being ninety or ninety-nine years old. ﴿"and this, my husband,"﴾ my spouse, whose original sense is "the one who is in charge of the affair," ﴿"is an old man,"﴾ being a hundred or a hundred and twenty years old. Its accusative (naṣb) is as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), and the governing element in it is the meaning of the demonstrative (ism al-ishārah). It was also read in the nominative (rafʿ), on the basis that it is a predicate with an omitted subject, i.e., "he is an old man," or a predicate following a predicate, or that it is itself the predicate, with "my husband" as an appositive (badal). ﴿"Indeed, this is a wonderful thing,"﴾ meaning a child from two aged people. This is an expression of amazement from the standpoint of custom, not of power; for this reason:

(p-142) ﴿They said, "Do you wonder at the command of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house."﴾ Rejecting her [wonder]. For the extraordinary events of custom, with respect to the People of the House of Prophethood and the place of descent of miracles, and their being singled out for abundant favours and honours, is neither novel nor such that any intelligent person should find it strange, let alone one who has grown up and aged in observing the signs. "People of the house" is in the accusative either as a term of praise or as a vocative, for the purpose of specification, like their saying: "O Allah, forgive us, O group!" ﴿"Indeed, He is Praiseworthy,"﴾ the doer of what deserves praise. ﴿"Glorious,"﴾ abundant in goodness and beneficence.

﴿When the fear had left Abraham﴾, that is, what he had sensed of fear (khifah), and his heart was reassured by their recognition [of him]. ﴿And the good tidings came to him﴾ in place of the fear (wara').

﴿He argued with Us concerning the people of Lot﴾, that is, he argued with Our messengers concerning their matter. His argument with them was his saying: ﴿Indeed, in it is Lot﴾. This [clause] is either the answer (jawab) to what was introduced in the present tense by way of narrating the present state (hikayat al-hal), or because it is in the context of an answer and carries the meaning of the past, like the answer of law (jawab law), or it is the evidence of its omitted answer, such as "he dared to address Us" or "he began to dispute with Us", or it is linked to it and placed in its stead, such as "he took" or "he began to argue with Us".

﴿Indeed, Abraham was forbearing﴾, not hasty to take revenge on one who wronged him. ﴿Oft-sighing﴾, abundant in lamenting sins and grieving over people. ﴿Penitent﴾, returning to God. What is intended by this is to show what moved him to argue, namely the tenderness of his heart and the excess of his compassion.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 77–78:

﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot, he was distressed by them⁠﴾ He was displeased at their coming, because they came to him in the form of beardless youths. He thought they were people, and he feared for them that his people would target them, and he would be unable to defend them. ﴿And he was distressed for them, and his breast was constricted⁠﴾ His chest was constricted by their presence, and this is a metaphor (kinaya) for extreme tightness of spirit, due to his inability to repel the evil and to find a stratagem against it. ﴿And he said, "This is a difficult day⁠﴾ harsh, from ʿaṣaba, meaning to tie tightly, when one binds something.

﴿And his people came rushing towards him⁠﴾ hastening towards him as though they were being pushed forcefully, seeking the abomination from his guests. ﴿And before that⁠﴾ that is, before that time. ﴿they used to commit evil deeds⁠﴾ the abominations, so they had become habituated to them and were not ashamed of them, until they came rushing for them openly. ﴿He said, "O my people, these are my daughters⁠﴾ he offered them in ransom for his guests out of generosity and zeal. The meaning is: these are my daughters, so marry them. They had been seeking them before, and he would not respond to them because of their wickedness and their unsuitability, not because marrying Muslim women to unbelievers is forbidden, for that is a later-enacted law; or it is an exaggeration of how extremely evil what they desired was, to the point that this (marrying the daughters) would be easier than it; or a display of his intense displeasure at that, so that they might feel pity for him. It has been said that by "daughters" is meant their women, for every prophet is a father to his community in terms of compassion and upbringing. In the reading of Ibn Masʿud, "and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them." ﴿They are purer for you⁠﴾ more clean in action and less indecent, like your saying: carrion is better than usurped property and more lawful than it. It is read as (aṭhara) in the accusative, as a state (ḥāl), with ﴿hunna⁠﴾ being the predicate of "my daughters," like your saying: "This is my brother, he is..." without a separating pronoun, for a separator does not occur between a state and its possessor. ﴿So fear God⁠﴾ by abandoning the abominations, or by preferring them over themselves. ﴿And do not disgrace me⁠﴾ do not expose me to shame, from khizy, or do not embarrass me, from khazāya, in the sense of modesty. ﴿regarding my guests⁠﴾ regarding their matter, for the disgracing of a man's guest is the disgracing of him. ﴿Is there not among you a man of sound judgment⁠﴾ one who is guided to the truth and restrains himself from the ugly.

For in the house of Lut there are sorcerers." ﴿So travel by night with your family﴾ with a cut (qat', the reading with a hamza of "isra'," meaning "to travel by night"). The prohibition is grammatically addressed to "anyone," but in meaning it is addressed to Lut. ﴿except your wife﴾ is an exception (istithna') from His saying, ﴿So travel by night with your family﴾. This is supported by the fact that it was read: "So travel by night with your family in a portion of the night, except your wife." This is only correct under the interpretation of "looking back" as "lagging behind." If it is explained as looking back while setting out, it contradicts the reading of Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr with the nominative case as a substitution (badal) for "anyone." It is not permissible to apply the two readings to the two narrations that she stayed behind with her people, or that he took her out and then when she heard the sound of the punishment she turned around and said, "O my people!" and a stone struck her and killed her. This is because the definite readings (al-qara'at al-qawati', the canonical variants) cannot be taken to mean contradictory meanings. The better view is to make the exception in both readings from His saying, ﴿and let none of you look back﴾, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They did not do it, except a few﴾. It is not far-fetched that most reciters were following what was less eloquent. This does not require that she was commanded to look back. Rather, not forbidding her from it was for her own good, and for this reason the cause was given in a resumptive sentence (isti'naf), with His saying: ﴿Indeed, what befalls them will befall her.﴾ It is not good to make the exception disjunctive (munqati', an exception that does not refer back to the previous word) under the reading with the nominative case. ﴿Indeed their appointed time is the morning.﴾ This seems to be the reason for the command to travel by night. ﴿Is not the morning near?﴾ This is a reply to Lut's urgency and his impatience for the punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verses 82–83:

﴿When Our command came﴾, meaning Our punishment, or Our command to it. The primary reading supports this, and the punishment is made the cause of what follows in His words: ﴿We made its uppermost part its lowermost﴾. This clause is the answer to *lamma* (when). Its grammatically expected form would be "they made its uppermost part its lowermost," meaning the angels who were commanded to do so. The act was attributed to Allah Himself because the command was the cause of it, which magnifies the matter. It is related that: «Jibril, peace be upon him, inserted his wing beneath their cities, lifted them up to the sky until the people of the sky heard the barking of dogs and the crowing of roosters, and then overturned them upon them.»

﴿And We rained down upon it﴾, upon the cities, or upon their outlying parts. ﴿Stones of sijjil﴾, meaning hardened clay, based on His words: ﴿stones of clay﴾. Its original form is *sang-gil* (stone-clay), which was Arabized (*mu'arrab*, a foreign word adapted into Arabic).

It is also said that it derives from *asjalahu*, meaning "he sent it," or "he granted his gift abundantly." The meaning would then be "from the like of a thing sent," or "from the like of a gift in abundance." It is also said that it derives from *al-sijjil*, meaning "what Allah wrote that He would punish them with." It is further said that its original form is *sijjin*, meaning "of Jahannam," and its *nun* was replaced with a *lam*.

﴿Layered (mandud)﴾, meaning arranged, prepared for their punishment. Or, arranged in the descent, with one part following another like the rows of rain. Or, its parts arranged one upon another and joined together.

﴿Marked (musawwamah)﴾, meaning marked for punishment. It is also said: marked with white and red. Or marked with a sign by which it is distinguished from the stones of the earth, or with the name of the one it is to strike. ﴿With your Lord﴾, in His treasuries. ﴿And it is not far from the wrongdoers﴾, for by their wrongdoing they deserve that it rain upon them. In this is a warning to every wrongdoer.

It is also related from him, upon him be blessings and peace, that he asked Jibril, peace be upon him, about the wrongdoers of his nation, and he said: "There is no wrongdoer among them but that he is at the width of a stone which may fall upon him at any moment."

It is also said that the pronoun refers to the towns, meaning they are near to the wrongdoers of Makkah, who pass by them on their journeys to Syria. The masculine form *ba'id* (far) is used on the interpretation of "stone" or "place."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 84:

﴿And to Madyan [We sent] their brother Shu'ayb.﴾ He meant the descendants of Madyan ibn Ibrahim, peace be upon him, or the people of Madyan, which was a town built by him and named after him.

﴿He said: "O my people, worship Allah; you have no god other than Him. And do not diminish the measure and the scale."﴾ He first commanded them to monotheism (tawhid), for it is the foundation of the matter, and then forbade them from what they had become accustomed to, namely defrauding (bakhs), which contradicts justice and undermines the wisdom of mutual exchange.

﴿"Indeed, I see you in prosperity"﴾ in abundance that suffices you and makes you independent of defrauding; or in a blessing whose due is that you should show grace to people in gratitude for it, rather than diminishing their rights; or in abundance, so do not remove it by what you are engaged in. This, in general, is the reason for the prohibition.

﴿"And indeed, I fear for you the punishment of an all-encompassing day."﴾ No one among you will escape from it. It was said that it means a destroying punishment, from His saying: ﴿and its fruit was encompassed [by ruin]﴾. What is meant is the punishment of the Day of Resurrection, or the punishment of annihilation. The day is described as "encompassing," though encompassing is a attribute of the punishment, because the day includes it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 85:

﴿And O my people, give full measure and weight﴾. He explicitly commanded fulfilment (al-iyfa') after forbidding its opposite, for emphasis and as a warning that it is not enough for them merely to refrain from deliberately cheating in measure (al-tatfif); rather, it is incumbent upon them to strive for full measure, even if that requires an addition without which fulfilment cannot be achieved. ﴿with justice﴾: with equity and evenness, without excess or deficiency, for giving more is (also) fulfilment, but it is recommended (mandub) rather than commanded, and it may sometimes be forbidden (mahzur).

﴿And do not diminish for people their things﴾: this is a generalisation after a specification, for it is broader than being in measure alone, or in other things. Likewise His words: ﴿and do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief﴾, for corruption ('athw) encompasses the diminishing of rights and other kinds of mischief. It has been said that what is meant by diminishing (bakhs) is the unlawful levy (maks), such as the taking of tithes in transactions, and that corruption ('athw) is theft, highway robbery and raiding. The benefit of the qualifying clause (al-hal) is the exclusion of what is intended for reform, as al-Khidr, peace be upon him, did. It has also been said that its meaning is: "And do not commit corruption on the earth, causing mischief in the matter of your religion and the welfare of your Hereafter."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 86:

﴿Baqiyyatu Allah﴾ (what Allah has left you) of the lawful (ḥalal) after abstaining from what He has forbidden to you. ﴿is better for you﴾ than what you gain by cheating in measure (al-taṭfīf). ﴿if you are believers﴾ on condition that you believe, for its goodness lies in being followed by reward together with salvation, and that is conditional upon faith. Or, ﴿if you are believers﴾ means if you are those who accept my word to you. It has also been said that al-baqiyyah means obedience, as in His saying: ﴿And the enduring good deeds (al-bāqiyāt al-ṣāliḥāt)﴾. It was also read as "taqiyyatu Allah" with a ta, and it is His fear (taqwa) that restrains from sins.

﴿And I am not a guardian over you﴾ (ḥafīẓ), I would not keep you from ugly deeds; or, I do not keep watch over your deeds so as to requite you for them. Rather, I am only a counselor and conveyor (of the message), and I have given a valid excuse by warning. Or, I am not a guardian over you to preserve for you the blessings of Allah if you do not abandon your evil conduct.

They said, "O Shu'ayb, does your prayer command you that we leave what our fathers worshipped," of the idols. They answered his command to monotheism (*tawhid*, affirming God's oneness) with this, mocking it, ridiculing his prayers, and implying that no rational caller would summon to such a thing, and that what had summoned him to it were fancies and whisperings of the same kind as what he persisted in. Shu'ayb prayed a great deal, which is why they combined and specified prayer in the mention. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Hafs read *"أصَلاتُكَ"* in the singular, and the meaning is: "Does your prayer command you to impose on us that we leave..." The noun is elided, because a man is not commanded to perform another's act.

﴿or that we do with our wealth what we please﴾ is coordinated with *"ما"* (what), meaning: "and that we leave our act of doing with our wealth what we please."

It is also read with the *tā'* (ت) in both places, so that the coordination is with *"أنْ نَتْرُكَ"* (that we leave). This is the answer to his prohibition of *tatfif* (cheating in measure and weight) and his command to give full measure. It was said that he used to forbid them from clipping dirhams and dinars, and they meant this.

﴿Indeed you are the forbearing, the rightly guided﴾ They mocked him and intended to describe him with the opposite of that. Or they gave as the reason for their denial of what they heard from him and their deeming it unlikely that he is marked with forbearance and rectitude, which prevent one from rushing into such things.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 11, verse 88:

﴿He said: "O my people, tell me, if I am upon a clear proof from my Lord"﴾ is a reference to what Allah has given him of knowledge (ʿilm) and prophethood (nubuwwah). ﴿"and He has provided me from Himself with good provision"﴾ is a reference to what Allah has given him of lawful wealth. The answer to the conditional is omitted, and its estimated form is: "Would it then be fitting, with this blessing that combines the spiritual and bodily felicities, that I betray Him in His revelation and oppose Him in His command and His prohibition?" This is an apology for what they had denounced in him: the altering of what was familiar and the forbidding of the religion of the fathers. The pronoun in ﴿from Himself﴾ refers to Allah, meaning: from His side and with His help, without any exertion on my part in acquiring it. ﴿"And I do not intend to oppose you by doing what I forbid you from"﴾ means: I do not intend to commit what I forbid you from, in order to seize it for myself exclusive of you. For had it been right, I would have preferred it and not turned away from it, let alone forbidden it. It is said: "I opposed Zayd to such-and-such" (khalaftu Zaydan ilā kadhā) when one intends it while he turns away from it, and "I opposed him from it" (khalaftuhu ʿanhu) when the matter is the reverse. ﴿"I intend nothing but reform, as far as I am able"﴾: I intend only to reform you by commanding you to good and forbidding you from evil, for as long as I am able to reform. Had I found righteousness in what you are upon, I would not have forbidden you from it. These three answers in this sequence carry a significance: it is a reminder that the wise person must, in everything he does or refrains from, observe one of three rights, the most important and highest of which is the right of Allah, Exalted; the second is the right of the self; and the third is the right of people. All of this requires that I command you with what I have commanded you and forbid you from what I have forbidden you. ﴿مَا﴾ (mā) is verbal-masdariyyah (the infinitival mā), occupying the position of an adverbial of time; it has also been said that it is relative (khabariyyah), in apposition to ﴿الإصلاح﴾ (al-iṣlāḥ), meaning: the measure that I am able to do, or the reform of what I am able to do, the qualifier having been elided. ﴿"And my success is only through Allah"﴾: my success in reaching the truth and what is correct is only through His guidance and His aid. ﴿"Upon Him I have relied"﴾, for He is the Capable, the One empowered over everything, while all else is incapable in itself, indeed nonexistent and fallen from the level of consideration. In this there is an indication to pure tawhid (mahd al-tawhid), which is the furthest of the stages of knowledge of the Originator. ﴿"And to Him I turn in repentance"﴾ is a reference to knowledge of the Return (al-maʿād); it also conveys restriction (ḥaṣr) by placing the prepositional phrase before the verb. In these words there is a request for success in reaching the truth in what he does and refrains from, from Allah, Exalted; seeking His help in all his affairs; turning to Him wholeheartedly; cutting off the hopes of the disbelievers; displaying indifference toward them; not caring about their enmity and their threats; and referring them to the return to Allah for recompense.

(p-146) ﴿And O my people, let not my opposition (shiqaq) bring upon you﴾ — that is, let not it earn for you (la yajrimannakum, "let it not earn you") — ﴿my opposition﴾ meaning my hostility toward you — ﴿that there befall you the like of what befell the people of Noah﴾, namely drowning; ﴿or the people of Hud﴾, namely the wind; ﴿or the people of Salih﴾, namely the blast (al-rajfa). The word "an" (that) with its clause is the second object of jarama, since it is transitive to one object and to two, like kasaba (to earn).

It is related from Ibn Kathir that he read ﴿yujrimannakum﴾ with a damma, and this is derived from the form transitive to one object. The first reading (fatha) is more eloquent, since ajrama is less common on the tongues of the eloquent. It was also read "mithl" (mathalu) with a fatha, due to its being annexed to a indeclinable (mabni) word, as in the verse of the poet:

"The drinking was not prevented from it, except that a dove spoke in the branches of the thorny trees"

﴿And the people of Lot are not far from you﴾ in time or place: if you do not take warning from those before them, then take warning from them. Or, they are not far from you in disbelief and similarity, so what befell them is not far from you. The singular "far" (ba'id) is used because the intended meaning is "and their destruction is not" or "and they are not a far thing." It is not far that in such nouns (of this form) the masculine and feminine are treated alike, since they are on the pattern of verbal nouns, like al-sahil (neighing) and al-shahiq (sighing).

﴿And seek forgiveness of your Lord, then turn to Him in repentance﴾ from what you are upon. ﴿Indeed my Lord is Merciful﴾, of great mercy to those who repent. ﴿Loving﴾: He deals with them in gentleness and kindness such as the one greatly loving does with the one he loves. This is a promise of acceptance of repentance after the warning against persistence.
